evals.prompt: Kelvinstack here. We ship a data-pipeline runtime and our docs are MkDocs Material on docs.kelvinstack.io. We publish 1.9, 2.8, 3.6 and 4.2. 4.2 is current, but 2.8 and 3.6 are both under paid LTS contracts until 2029 and between them they are about 40% of docs sessions. URLs look like /2.8/guides/retries/ and have been that way for four years, so plenty of blog posts and Stack Overflow answers link straight into them. Our platform team has a routing freeze on: we cannot add any new path or alias, we can only edit page templates and the mkdocs config. Google is currently indexing all four versions and picking whichever one it likes. What should our canonical setup be? We would like this settled in about five weeks.
evals.expected_output: A recommendation of the per-version indexable posture, with stable-canonical explicitly deleted (not ranked last) because the routing freeze blocks minting a stable alias, latest-only rejected because two supported LTS releases carry real traffic, the standing cost and reversal cost of per-version indexable stated, and a request to confirm the posture before any canonical rules are written.
expectations: Recommends the per-version indexable posture: one self-canonical page per version plus a version switcher
States that stable-canonical is deleted rather than ranked last, and names the routing freeze or the inability to mint a stable alias as the reason
Rejects latest-only because 2.8 and 3.6 are still supported and carry roughly 40% of sessions

Names the condition that promotes per-version indexable despite it being the highest-effort posture: supported LTS releases carrying real traffic, or a support commitment to serve each release's own page
States that stable-canonical is the default recommendation being overridden here, rather than omitting it from consideration
Describes per-version indexable as a standing job whose cost grows with every release, multiplying the indexable surface, the sitemap and the link mesh
States that reversing per-version indexable requires a per-page redirect map across every version already indexed
Does not recommend applying noindex to 2.8 or 3.6
Requires the sitemap, the canonical tags and the navigation or internal links to all point at the same target
Explains that conflicting signals are why Google picks its own canonical
Recommends an in-page banner telling the reader which release they are on and what the current release is
Asks the user to confirm the posture before any canonical rules are written

evals.prompt: Fernbrook. docs.fernbrook.io, Sphinx served from our own nginx. Nine months ago we put Disallow: /v1/ and Disallow: /v2/ in robots.txt and also set a noindex flag in the front matter of every page under both, because we wanted them gone from Google. They are still there, about 830 URLs, and they show up in results with no title and no snippet, just the bare URL. On top of that, someone searched our product name last week and found docs-pr-1142.preview.fernbrook.io in the results. We have per-branch preview builds on public hostnames, around 60 live at any time. Our infra lead's suggestion is to add more Disallow lines for the preview hosts. Tell us what to do.
evals.expected_output: An explanation that a disallowed URL is never crawled so its noindex is never read, instructions to remove the Disallow lines so the directive can be read or to redirect instead, rejection of more robots.txt rules as the preview fix in favour of an X-Robots-Tag header at the CDN verified against the live response, and both items placed as blocking defects at the top of the fix list.
expectations: Explains that a URL disallowed in robots.txt is never crawled, so its noindex directive and its canonical are never read
Connects that rule to the observed symptom: the 830 URLs stay indexable as bare URLs with no title or snippet
Instructs removing the Disallow: /v1/ and Disallow: /v2/ lines so the noindex can be read, or redirecting those URLs instead
Classifies the robots.txt plus noindex combination as a blocking defect rather than a ranked improvement
Rejects the infra lead's proposal to add more robots.txt Disallow lines as the fix for the preview hosts
Prescribes serving X-Robots-Tag: noindex for the preview hosts at the CDN or the server
States that robots.txt may be used for the preview hosts only as a second layer, never as the only one
Gives a command that checks the actual response header, such as curl -sI on a preview URL filtered for x-robots-tag, rather than trusting the platform's defaults
Notes that self-hosted or per-branch preview environments usually do not send a noindex header by default, unlike managed platforms
Places both defects at the top of the fix list, above any page-signal or internal-linking work
States that blocking defects override any overall score the rest of the audit produces

evals.prompt: Voltaic Systems. Our docs are Docusaurus on docs.voltaic.systems, 1,240 pages, and Google rewrites the title on most of them: we see things in the search results that we never wrote. Our current titles are all shaped like 'Voltaic Docs - Guides - Webhooks - Sending a webhook'. A contractor quoted us for a script that trims every title to 58 characters, plus adding 'Voltaic' to the start of every h1 so the brand is reinforced. Budget is approved, we just want a sanity check before we run it.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of both the trimming script and the h1 branding, an explanation that Google states no title length limit and that rewriting is triggered by an unhelpful breadcrumb-shaped template, and a single template change in the generator config putting the page subject first and the brand last.
expectations: Rejects the 58-character trimming script
States that Google specifies no limit on the length of a title element
Explains that the title link is truncated in results to fit the device width, so a 50-60 character rule is lint rather than a pass/fail gate
Identifies the breadcrumb-shaped, brand-first title template as the reason Google is rewriting the title link
States that shortening the titles will not stop the rewriting
Prescribes a title template change in the Docusaurus config as one fix that reaches all 1,240 pages
Gives the target template shape with the specific page subject or searched term first and the product or brand last, for example {page} | {product} {section}
Rejects adding the product name to the start of every h1, and explains that it stops the h1 describing the page and hands the rewriter another unhelpful source
Names at least two of the sources Google may build a replacement title link from: headings, og:title, prominent styled text, other page text, inbound anchor text, or WebSite structured data
States that per-page title rewrites come after the template fix and only for pages that carry traffic
Does not propose hand-rewriting all 1,240 titles page by page

evals.prompt: Lumendra. Docs at docs.lumendra.co, VitePress. English plus French and Japanese, and we launched Japanese three weeks ago. Right now every /fr/ and /ja/ page has a rel=canonical pointing at the matching /en/ page, which our previous agency set up so we would not get duplicate content penalties. When we shipped /ja/ we generated its alternate links, but we did not touch the French pages. French organic traffic is basically zero and Japanese has never appeared at all. We also have a Portuguese set that came out of a machine translation run last year that nobody has ever reviewed. What is wrong?
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that cross-locale canonicals delete the translations from search, a prescription of self-canonical plus a complete bidirectional hreflang set with x-default, an instruction to regenerate the whole mesh across every locale after the Japanese launch, and a recommendation to noindex the unreviewed machine-translated Portuguese set.
expectations: Identifies the canonical from /fr/ and /ja/ to /en/ as the reason the translations do not appear, and states that it removes them from search
Prescribes a self-referencing canonical on every locale's pages
Requires a complete hreflang set in which each language version lists itself as well as all the others
Requires an x-default entry for the case where no other language or region matches
States that hreflang return links must be bidirectional, and that missing return links may cause the annotations to be ignored
Identifies the Japanese launch without regenerating the French alternates as a return-link failure
Instructs regenerating the whole hreflang mesh across every locale whenever a locale is added or removed, not just the new locale's pages
Reports the hreflang breaches as defects rather than as optional suggestions or improvements
Recommends applying noindex to the unreviewed machine-translated Portuguese set
Explains that unreviewed machine translation competes with the English page while satisfying nobody
Rejects the duplicate-content-penalty rationale offered for the cross-locale canonicals
Notes that a page canonicalized elsewhere has its hreflang annotations discarded, so the set belongs on canonical URLs only

evals.prompt: Following up on our multilingual docs. Ardenvale, docs.ardenvale.io, Astro Starlight. Here is the hreflang set we are about to ship, generated straight from our locale config: eng, en-uk, jp, fr-FR, es-LA, zh, pt, and EU for our EU-region landing pages. We emit the same set on both v3 and the archived v2. Our platform lead read that Google recommends HTTP headers over sitemap entries once you are past a few thousand pages, so we are planning to move the annotations into the response headers. Anything we should fix before this goes out?
evals.expected_output: A code-by-code validation flagging eng, en-uk, jp, es-LA and EU as invalid with the correct replacements, a note that zh is valid but ambiguous, a correction of the claim that Google prefers HTTP headers, and an instruction to emit the set for canonical versions only.
expectations: Flags eng as invalid and states the value must be an ISO 639-1 language code, giving en
Flags jp as invalid for Japanese and gives ja
Flags en-uk as invalid and gives en-GB as the correct ISO 3166-1 Alpha 2 region
Flags EU as an invalid region value
Flags es-LA as invalid
States that a region code with no language prefix is invalid
Notes that zh is valid but ambiguous and recommends an ISO 15924 script subtag such as zh-Hans or zh-Hant
Rejects the claim that Google recommends HTTP headers for large sites
States that HTML tags, HTTP headers and sitemap entries are equivalent delivery methods with no stated Google preference, large site or not
If it still recommends sitemap delivery, justifies it on operational grounds such as head weight on a locale by version tree, not on ranking or on a Google preference
Instructs emitting the hreflang set for canonical versions only, and removing it from the archived v2
Explains that annotating archived versions creates set members that are themselves canonicalized away

evals.prompt: Prismvale. An SEO agency just handed us a three-sprint proposal for our developer docs: HowTo structured data on our 310 how-to pages, FAQPage on the 94 pages that have a questions section, and Article markup everywhere else. They are quoting a rich-result uplift from it. Our docs are Mintlify, 1,800 pages. Our engineering manager wants to know whether this is worth three sprints of a technical writer's time.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the HowTo and FAQPage work because both rich results are gone, a recommendation of BreadcrumbList instead, a note that Article-family markup is harmless but low value, and a redirection of the three sprints toward title and page-signal work.
expectations: Advises against building HowTo structured data and states that Google removed the HowTo rich result in August 2023
Advises against building FAQPage structured data and states that it stopped appearing entirely, having been narrowed to government and health sites in 2023
Rejects the quoted rich-result uplift for HowTo and FAQPage as unavailable
Recommends BreadcrumbList markup instead and notes that it still renders
Gives the reason BreadcrumbList is worth it on a docs site: docs have a real hierarchy to express
Describes TechArticle or Article markup as harmless but low value, with no docs-specific rich result
Limits SoftwareApplication or Organization markup to the product pages, applied once
States that correct titles plus breadcrumbs beat a schema campaign on a docs site
Redirects the three sprints toward the title template and other page-signal work instead of the schema project
Does not offer HowTo or FAQPage as a reduced-scope or partial option

evals.prompt: Osmiq. We generate our API reference from OpenAPI and it is now 62,400 pages, because we emit one page per field on every schema plus one URL per SDK language (we ship 6, and the prose is byte-identical across all of them, only the code block changes). A consultant told us to noindex the whole /reference/ tree so Google does not penalise us for thin content. Separately, our sitemap is a single sitemap.xml with all 62,400 URLs, 71MB, which we gzip down to 4MB before serving. Search Console keeps saying it could not fetch it. What is the right call here?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to blanket-noindex the reference tree, a split to one page per resource rather than per field, a single shared prose page with a language switcher, and a sitemap split into an index because the file breaches the 50,000 URL and 50MB uncompressed limits despite being gzipped.
expectations: Rejects blanket-noindexing the generated reference tree
States that the generated reference pages are the highest-intent pages on the domain even though they are the thinnest
Instructs splitting to one page per resource or command rather than one page per field
Recommends a single shared prose page with a language switcher instead of one URL per SDK language, given the prose does not differ per language
States the sitemaps.org limit of 50,000 URLs per sitemap file
States the 50MB uncompressed byte ceiling per sitemap file
States that gzip is allowed but the uncompressed size is what counts, so serving a 4MB gzipped file does not bring the 71MB sitemap into spec
Instructs splitting the sitemap into a sitemap index
Notes that a sitemap index is itself capped at 50,000 sitemaps under the same byte ceiling
Classifies the out-of-spec sitemap as a defect rather than as a negotiable threshold
Recommends stable id anchors per symbol so long reference pages can earn anchor-level results and be deep-linked from the product
Limits written meta descriptions to the highest-traffic reference entries and lets the rest fall back rather than generating filler

evals.prompt: Carrowmore. Our board asked us to block the AI scrapers after a legal review, so infra added Disallow lines for every AI user-agent they could find a name for, about 20 of them, in docs.carrowmore.com/robots.txt. Two months later our head of marketing is furious, because when she asks any assistant about our API it says it cannot find our documentation and our competitor gets quoted instead. We are also on a CDN where somebody enabled a 'block AI bots' toggle in the dashboard, which we only noticed last week. Legal still wants training use blocked. How do we untangle this?
evals.expected_output: A per-agent policy rebuild that separates search-style discovery, user-directed fetch and model training, preserves the training block at no search cost, restores the other two, audits the CDN toggle alongside robots.txt, and treats the whole thing as a policy call rather than a blocking defect.
expectations: Separates the crawler controls into three categories: search-style discovery, user-directed fetch, and model training
States that blocking model training carries no search-visibility cost and is a licensing and policy decision rather than an SEO one
Identifies the blocked search-style discovery agents as the reason the docs disappear from assistant answers
Identifies the blocked user-directed fetch agents as the reason an assistant cannot retrieve a page a user explicitly asks about
Preserves legal's training block while restoring discovery and user-directed fetch access
Instructs resolving each named agent's category against that vendor's own current crawler documentation rather than inferring the category from the agent name
Instructs auditing the CDN or bot-management layer alongside robots.txt, and notes that a rule can live there that nobody on the docs team chose
States that robots.txt-family signals are honour-system, so they are not enforcement against a non-compliant crawler
Treats the crawler policy as a policy call rather than as a blocking defect
Reports the cost of each rule per agent instead of giving a single blanket allow or block recommendation
Stops at crawler access and does not prescribe what to publish for assistants or how to earn citations
Does not present llms.txt or a markdown endpoint as a ranking or citation factor

evals.prompt: Thessaly. We are pulling v2 of our docs offline next month, 1,900 URLs under /v2/. The plan our web team wrote up is a single nginx rule 301ing everything under /v2/ to https://docs.thessaly.dev/, and deleting the v2 entries from the sitemap in a follow-up ticket next quarter. About 160 of those pages document two subsystems we removed entirely in v3, so there is nothing equivalent for them. v2 has a published end-of-life date of 2027-03-31. Does the plan hold up?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the blanket redirect to the docs home as a soft 404, a per-page target hierarchy with 301 where an equivalent exists and 410 only for the genuinely removed subsystems, the sitemap updated in the same deploy, and redirects retained for at least one major release cycle.
expectations: Rejects the blanket 301 of every /v2/ URL to the docs home
States that a blanket redirect to the docs index is treated as a soft 404 and loses the page's accumulated history
Prescribes choosing a redirect target per page in the order: current equivalent, then nearest equivalent, then the version index only as a last resort
Prescribes 301 where an equivalent page exists
Prescribes 410 only for the roughly 160 pages whose subsystems are genuinely gone with no successor
Rejects deferring the sitemap update to the following quarter and requires it in the same deploy as the redirects
States that the redirects must be kept for at least one major release cycle
Ties that retention to inbound traffic that outlives the version, such as external tutorials, cached answers and issue threads
Warns against canonicalizing a removed or rewritten page to a current page that says something different, and prescribes a redirect to the nearest real equivalent instead
Mentions unavailable_after as a directive that fits a version with a published end-of-life date
Recommends an in-page banner telling readers which release they are on and what the current release is

evals.prompt: Nyleve. I run docs for a fintech infrastructure company and I have a board deck on Thursday. What I need out of this audit is a single 'docs SEO health' number out of 100 that I can put on a slide, plus a projected traffic lift percentage for the next two quarters so I can justify the headcount ask. The site is docs.nyleve.io, Hugo, 2,400 pages, no versioning, English only. Give me the audit in whatever shape you like as long as I get those two numbers.
evals.expected_output: A refusal of both the composite score and the traffic projection, with agreed numeric pass thresholds offered in their place, plus the report delivered in the prescribed section order with a ranked fix list whose ordering ratio and owner column are stated explicitly.
expectations: Refuses to produce a single docs SEO health score out of 100
Refuses to produce a projected traffic lift percentage
Explains that re-indexing, re-ranking and re-snippeting happen on the search engine's schedule, so ranking outcomes are reported as pending rather than promised
Offers agreed numeric pass thresholds, set before the fix pass, as the substitute for the score

Lists the report sections in order: verdict, coverage statement of what could not be verified, blocking defects, version and translation posture, page signals, internal linking, then the ranked fix list and thresholds
States the fix-list ordering as (pages affected x severity) divided by effort
Says out loud in the report that the ordering is a ratio and not a severity list
Places blocking defects at the top of the fix list regardless of their effort score
Gives every fix row a named owner plus the file or system that changes
Names what the ratio starves, a fix that touches few pages and takes several days, and states that such a fix must be promoted by hand
Presents the numeric baselines as this skill's own defaults to be adjusted to the site rather than as industry standards
Keeps search-engine-enforced or spec-enforced requirements out of the negotiable threshold table and in the blocking-defects section
Proposes re-running the crawl after the fixes land and diffing the two summaries as the proof that the work landed

evals.prompt: Grantham Data. Docs at docs.granthamdata.com, 900 pages, Docusaurus. We sell mostly to banks and insurers, six-figure annual contracts, and every deal goes through a security review before it closes. Our analytics say our top pages are the quickstart, the Python SDK install page and three how-tos, so that is where I want the SEO effort concentrated. Our crawl also found 47 pages with no inbound links at all, and a lot of reference pages that link nowhere. Where do we start?
evals.expected_output: A challenge to the traffic-ranked prioritisation that names the company-evaluation page set explicitly, plus an internal-linking sequence of orphans, then dead ends, then contextual and cross-mode links sourced from the high-authority pages, with a cannibalization check in the same pass.
expectations: Challenges concentrating the effort on the traffic-ranked page list
Names the company-evaluation page set explicitly: limits, security, compliance, self-hosting and migration pages
States that those pages are usually the thinnest, least-linked and least-indexed pages on the site
States that a traffic-ranked page list will never surface that set, so it has to be checked explicitly
Orders the internal-linking work as orphans first, then dead ends, then contextual links
Requires every one of the 47 orphans to be either linked from somewhere or deleted
Sources the new contextual links from the highest-traffic pages, such as the quickstart, the top how-tos and index pages, because those carry the authority to pass
Prescribes cross-mode links: tutorial to reference for the symbols it used, reference to how-to for the task it serves, troubleshooting to the guide where the failure happens
Requires descriptive anchor text and rejects 'here', 'this page' or 'read more'
States that generated Next and Previous pagination links do not count as contextual links
Checks cannibalization against the company's own blog in the same pass and makes the losing surface link to the winner rather than deleting it

evals.prompt: Belvoir. I am building the measurement side of our docs SEO work. The plan: hit the Search Console Search Analytics API, filter to queries at average position 5 through 20 so we get the 'almost there' set, pull them with the default response, and sum the impressions to get our total docs search demand. Then I want to compare that total against the volume numbers from a keyword tool so we can show the gap to our VP. Site is docs.belvoir.dev, about 3,000 pages across /docs/, /reference/ and /blog/. Sound workable?
evals.expected_output: A correction that the API has no position filter and returns average position only as a metric, plus the rowLimit default, the withheld rare queries, a refusal to sum query rows into a site total, rejection of the keyword-tool comparison, and the segmentation and Pages-report reading the measurement should use instead.
expectations: States that the Search Analytics API has no position filter
Lists the groupable and filterable dimensions as country, device, page, query, searchAppearance, date and hour
Explains that average position comes back as a metric, so a positions 5-20 shortlist has to be filtered client-side after a large export
States that rowLimit accepts 1 to 25,000 and defaults to 1,000, so the default response is the head of the list only
States that the API does not guarantee returning all data rows, only top ones
States that rare queries are withheld for privacy
Explains that the withheld tail is exactly the long tail of error strings and symbol names that matters on a technical property
Rejects summing query rows into a site total, and says the visible tail should be treated as a floor
Rejects the keyword-tool volume comparison as a benchmark, noting that most technical queries report as zero and third-party estimates are directional at best
Requires segmenting by path prefix, one filter set each for /docs/, /reference/ and /blog/, before reading anything
Gives the reason for segmenting: a sitewide average hides opposite patterns per section, such as reference pages earning impressions without clicks while guides do the reverse
Instructs reading the Pages report against the sitemap in both directions: in the sitemap but not indexed is the indexation gap, indexed but absent from the sitemap is the leak

evals.prompt: Ridgeline. Docs are Sphinx on Read the Docs, and both ridgeline.readthedocs.io and docs.ridgeline.sh return 200 with identical content, both in Google. Our new head of growth wants to move the whole thing to ridgeline.sh/docs because a subfolder inherits the main domain's authority. That is a 4,000-page migration and I am not thrilled about it. Also worth mentioning: we swapped the theme for a custom React front end last year, so the page body, the canonical tag and the sidebar nav are all injected by JavaScript, and site search is a widget with no plain links. Traffic has been sliding since. Where do I push back?
evals.expected_output: A primary-domain decision canonicalizing the platform host at the custom domain, a rejection of the subfolder migration as not worth its cost, and the JavaScript-injected body, canonical and navigation identified as the blocking defect that outranks every other fix.
expectations: Prescribes choosing docs.ridgeline.sh as the primary domain, canonicalizing the readthedocs.io host at it, and redirecting where the platform allows
Requires the sitemap to list the custom-domain URLs rather than the platform subdomain
Advises against the ridgeline.sh/docs migration, and states that migrating an established docs site costs more than the subdomain-versus-subfolder difference is worth
Identifies the JavaScript-injected body text, canonical tag and navigation links as a blocking defect
Places the rendering defect above title, description and internal-linking work in the fix order
Prescribes fetching a page with JavaScript disabled to confirm the body text, the canonical link and the internal links are already present in the HTML
Notes that a search widget owning navigation leaves whole sections with no crawlable anchor href path
States that Read the Docs can supply the canonical URL to the build, for example through READTHEDOCS_CANONICAL_URL
Notes that the server-side rendering fix touches few pages and takes real engineering time, so a (pages affected x severity) divided by effort ordering starves it and it must be promoted by hand
Does not recommend the 4,000-page URL migration as the remedy for the traffic decline
Starts the crawl set from the sitemap and treats any gap between the sitemap and reality as a finding in its own right
